authoringProvenance.author: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Pro candidate authoring; human review required

items.prompt: Order the core steps of recursive graph DFS for a preorder-style visit of vertex u. The graph may contain cycles.

elements.text: Process u for the preorder visit.
For each unvisited neighbor v, recurse into DFS(v).

feedback.reason: DFS must claim the vertex before following an edge that could lead back to it.

blocks.text: Claim the vertex before descending

items: Mark u visited immediately, so an edge back to u cannot open another active DFS(u) frame.
Process u now because the requested visit is preorder: parent work occurs before child work.
Iterate through u's outgoing neighbors.
For each neighbor v that is still unvisited, call DFS(v); already-visited neighbors are skipped.

blocks.text: For a cycle u → v → u, marking u first makes the second edge observe u as visited and terminate that route. Moving the processing callback after all recursive children would produce postorder rather than the requested preorder, but marking must still precede descent in either form.

blocks.title: Active-frame invariant
blocks.text: Every active graph-DFS frame owns a vertex already marked discovered; only unseen neighbors create child frames.

items.prompt: An iterative DFS uses an explicit stack. A vertex can be reached from several already-discovered vertices. Which policy best avoids pushing the same vertex many times?

options.text: Leave it unvisited until popped; marking on pop is always equivalent.
Switch to an adjacency matrix; duplicate pushes occur only with adjacency lists.
When an unseen neighbor is pushed, mark it discovered immediately.
Record only the first parent and skip visited state because DFS always creates a tree.

feedback.reason: Discovery should be recorded when the stack accepts the vertex, so later incoming edges see it as already claimed.

blocks.text: Discovered means accepted as pending work

Consider a triangle A—B—C—A. After A pushes unmarked B and C, suppose C is popped first. If B is still considered unvisited until its own pop, C can push a second copy of B even though the first copy is already pending.

items: Push the start vertex and mark it discovered.
Pop one vertex for processing.
For each neighbor not yet discovered, mark it immediately and push it once.
Ignore later incoming edges to that already-claimed vertex.

blocks.title: Processed and discovered are different states
blocks.text: A vertex may be discovered and waiting on the stack before it is processed. Delayed processing is safe only if a separate discovered or pending set still prevents duplicate pushes.

blocks.title: Stack invariant
blocks.text: Mark on push so each vertex has at most one canonical pending stack entry.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mark_on_pop: Several predecessors can push the same still-unmarked vertex before its first pop, creating duplicate stack entries and extra work.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.matrix_fix: Duplicate discovery is controlled by visited timing, not by whether neighbors come from a list or matrix.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.tree_parent_only: The traversal tree is an output of discovery; the input graph can contain cross edges and cycles that still require discovered-state checks.

items.prompt: The task is to report every vertex reachable from source s in an unweighted graph; no shortest distance or level order is requested. Which statement is correct?

options.text: DFS is valid only with an adjacency matrix.
BFS is required because BFS is always faster than DFS.
DFS may omit visited state because its recursive calls form a tree.
DFS is valid because any complete cycle-safe exploration of s’s reachable region produces the required set.

feedback.reason: Reachable-set output requires complete exploration, not a particular layer order.

blocks.text: Reachability needs exhaustive exploration, not distance order

Starting from s, DFS repeatedly takes one unseen neighbor and follows that branch as deeply as possible, then backtracks to try remaining neighbors. Because every discovered vertex is marked and every outgoing edge of every reached vertex is eventually inspected, the result is exactly the set reachable from s.

items: An adjacency list supports this traversal in O(Vr + Er), where Vr and Er are the reached vertices and their inspected outgoing edges.
A matrix or implicit neighbor generator can also support DFS; the representation changes access cost, not DFS legality.
BFS reaches the same set but additionally processes it by nondecreasing edge distance.

blocks.title: Selection boundary
blocks.text: DFS is sufficient for a complete reachable set; choose BFS when minimum unweighted distance or level order is part of the output.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.bfs_required: Both traversals inspect the reachable vertices and edges under the same representation; no shortest-path contract selects BFS here.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.matrix_required: DFS needs neighbor access but is independent of a specific representation; lists, matrices, or implicit neighbors can support it.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.tree_no_visited: The call tree does not remove cycles and cross edges from the input graph.

items.prompt: A graph is a single path of 2,000,000 vertices. The language runtime has a shallow call-stack limit. Which DFS implementation decision addresses the material risk without changing reachability semantics?

options.text: Build an adjacency matrix so recursion cannot overflow.
Replace DFS with BFS because BFS is always faster.
Use iterative DFS with an explicit stack and the same visited invariant.
Keep recursion but mark a vertex only when returning from it.

feedback.reason: A path can create Θ(V) recursive depth, so an explicit stack moves that state to controlled heap memory.

blocks.text: Replace call frames, not DFS semantics

items: Recursive DFS on a two-million-vertex path can create Θ(V) nested calls before any call returns.
A shallow runtime call stack may overflow long before those two million frames fit.
Iterative DFS stores pending vertices in an explicit stack and keeps the same mark-before-push discovery rule.

blocks.text: The conversion avoids the fixed call-stack limit; it does not claim constant auxiliary space. Explicit pending state and visited state can still use O(V) memory in a general graph. A matrix changes edge storage but leaves recursive depth untouched, while marking on return makes cycles unsafe and also leaves the path depth unchanged.

blocks.title: Implementation boundary
blocks.text: When recursion depth can exceed the runtime limit, implement the same DFS invariant with an explicit stack.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.bfs_faster: The issue is recursion depth, not a universal runtime ranking; iterative DFS preserves the intended depth-first behavior.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.matrix_storage: Representation does not remove recursive call depth and would add prohibitive quadratic storage.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mark_on_return: On a graph with cycles this is unsafe, and it does not reduce the path’s call depth.

items.prompt: An unweighted graph contains paths s → a → b → t and s → x → t. A DFS explores neighbor a before x and stops when it first reaches t. What is wrong with using that result as the shortest path?

options.text: Nothing; DFS reaches a terminal vertex as soon as possible and is therefore shortest.
First DFS discovery follows depth order, so it may return the three-edge path before the two-edge path.
The result is wrong only because an adjacency list was used instead of a matrix.
Marking t only after unwinding the recursion would make the first path shortest.

feedback.reason: DFS first discovery is governed by neighbor order and depth, not by minimum edge count.

blocks.text: First in depth order is not first in distance order

items: DFS follows the first listed branch s → a → b → t and reaches t after three edges.
Because it stops immediately, it never examines the sibling branch beginning with x.
That sibling contains s → x → t, which reaches the same target in two edges.

blocks.text: DFS therefore returns a valid path but cannot certify minimum edge count. BFS would process s, then all one-edge states {a, x}, then two-edge states including t, so its first discovery of t has distance two. Changing adjacency storage or visited timing cannot turn depth order into layer order.

blocks.title: Output-contract rule
blocks.text: A first-found DFS path proves reachability only; minimum unweighted edge count requires nondecreasing-distance exploration.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.dfs_always_shortest: Depth-first exploration minimizes neither edge count nor accumulated weight.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.matrix_needed: Neighbor storage can alter tie order but does not give DFS a shortest-path guarantee.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mark_on_pop_fix: Visited timing does not turn depth-first order into nondecreasing distance order.

items.prompt: A graph has three disconnected regions. A correct DFS is called once from a vertex in the first region. Which conclusion is valid?

options.text: Only BFS can continue into the other regions because BFS is always faster.
Recursive DFS eventually reaches all declared vertices even without edges between regions.
That call visits exactly the vertices reachable from its start; whole-graph coverage needs an outer scan over unvisited vertices.
The DFS parent tree implicitly connects the regions, so no outer scan is needed.

feedback.reason: A DFS call is bounded by reachability from its start vertex.

blocks.text: One start is confined to one reachable region
DFS can move only along graph edges. With no path from the first region to either of the other two, the call visits exactly the first start's reachable set and then its stack becomes empty.

items: Scan every declared vertex.
Skip a vertex already visited by an earlier DFS.
When an unvisited vertex appears, start another DFS to cover that region.
After the scan, every declared vertex has been covered.

blocks.title: Traversal cannot invent a bridge
blocks.text: Neither recursion, BFS, nor the DFS parent tree creates an edge between disconnected regions. A new outer-loop start is required.

blocks.title: Invocation scope
blocks.text: One DFS covers one start's reachable set; whole-graph coverage requires an outer scan of unvisited vertices.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.all_graph: Traversal follows edges and cannot cross a disconnected boundary.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.bfs_only_components: Neither traversal can cross absent edges; both require a new start for each unseen region.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.tree_parent_bridge: Traversal parents are created only for reached vertices and cannot invent missing graph edges.

items.prompt: Two correct DFS implementations use the same start vertex and visited rule but iterate each adjacency list in a different order. What may differ?

options.text: Any difference disappears if both mark visited only after popping or returning.
The reachable set changes because DFS correctness depends on one canonical neighbor order.
The results match only if both implementations use an adjacency matrix.
The DFS tree and visitation sequence may differ, while the reachable set remains the same.

feedback.reason: DFS traversal order is occurrence-specific, but complete cycle-safe exploration preserves reachability.

blocks.text: Neighbor order chooses the witness, not the reachable set

Suppose s has neighbors a and b and both can reach c. An implementation that examines a first may assign c's DFS parent through a; one that examines b first may assign it through b. Their visitation sequences, parent edges, and discovery or finish timestamps can therefore differ.

Both implementations still inspect every unvisited neighbor eventually, so each discovers every vertex reachable from s. A matrix does not force a semantic order, and late marking does not remove order dependence; it can instead introduce duplicate work or unsafe cycle behavior.

blocks.title: Determinism boundary
blocks.text: If output order or a specific DFS tree matters, declare and enforce a neighbor order; otherwise multiple DFS witnesses are valid.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.reachability_changes: For complete exploration, neighbor order affects which path discovers a vertex first, not whether a reachable vertex is eventually discovered.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.matrix_equivalence: Representation and neighbor order are separate; either representation can enumerate neighbors in different valid orders.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.late_mark_equivalence: Late marking can introduce duplicate work or cycles and is not a remedy for nondeterministic neighbor order.
